q-80372.name: Question 1
q-80372.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-80372.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1

Consider the matrix A=[68−4−6]. You're given that λ1=2 and λ2=−2 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[2−1], v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[200−2] and P=[2−1−11]
b
D=[02−20] and P=[2−11−11]
c
D=[2−200] and P=[21−1−1]
d
D=[02−20] and P=[2−1−11]
e
D=[−2002] and P=[21−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=2 and λ2=−2, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[200−2].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2.

Therefore, we get

P=[2−1−11].

q-80391.problem:
Consider the matrix $E=[\begin{aligned}-32 & 40 \\ -30 & 38\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8$ are the eigenvalues of $E$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=E,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
q-80391.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=8.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix E=[−3240−3038]. You're given that λ1=−2 and λ2=8 are the eigenvalues of E, and v1=[43], v2=[22] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=E, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[200−8] and P=[3242]
b
D=[800−2] and P=[4232]
c
D=[−2008] and P=[4232]
d
D=[−2800] and P=[4−232]
e
D=[800−2] and P=[2432]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−2 and λ2=8, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−2008].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=8.

Therefore, we get

P=[4232].

q-80455.name: Question 3
q-80455.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -12 \\ 4 & -7\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
q-80455.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -12 \\ 4 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-4\cdot (-12) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

q-80464.name: Question 4
q-80464.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 2 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
q-80464.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

q-140053.name: Question 5
q-140053.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$
q-140053.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$
